html:
The northern Syrian city of Aleppo in the 16th century, when it became a great hub of caravan trade inside the Ottoman Empire. The Ottomans won it in 1516 by beating the Mamluks nearby, and the next year conquered Egypt.

Aleppo stood where caravan routes from Persia, Iraq and the Persian Gulf met the roads to the Mediterranean. Raw silk from Safavid Iran was its main export, along with spices, cotton and dyes. Merchants from Venice, France and later England and the Netherlands set up consulates and lived in its great inns, the khans. Its covered markets stretched for kilometres. It was the third city of the empire after Istanbul and Cairo.

The French historian Fernand Braudel saw the Ottoman Empire of this time as a world economy of its own, largely self-contained, with its own routes, coins and markets. Aleppo was one of its centres. Its trade faded in the 17th and 18th centuries as ships carried goods around Africa and the port of Izmir rose. Aleppo had survived disasters before, such as the earthquake of 1138.
